strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies judge heterogeneity as a fundamental source of bias in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, with compelling observation that more data can make rankings more confidently wrong under misspecification

Rigorous theoretical contributions: Establishes identifiability up to natural normalizations, proves consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE, enabling principled confidence intervals for score differences and rank comparisons

Strong simulation validation: Section 4 effectively validates theoretical predictions, including O(1/T) convergence rates and correct confidence interval coverage, while demonstrating systematic under-coverage of the unweighted baseline

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments on MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and an in-house dataset with 45 models consistently demonstrate alignment with established benchmarks and improved data efficiency
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with intuitive model exposition, logical flow from motivation to theory to experiments, and effective use of figures to communicate results
Practical relevance: Addresses an increasingly important problem in LLM evaluation infrastructure with clear deployment potential for improving leaderboard reliability
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The core contribution (adding multiplicative discrimination parameters to BTL) is a straightforward extension of Otani et al. (2016). While application to fully randomized reference-free LLM evaluation is novel, the conceptual advance is incremental and standard MLE asymptotic theory applies

Critical missing comparisons: No comparison with existing methods REM (Yang et al., 2024), GTR/FTR (Dhurandhar et al., 2024), or Product-of-Experts aggregation (Fathullah & Gales, 2025) on the same datasets. Only compares against unweighted BTL baseline, limiting assessment of relative performance

Weak validation against human preferences: Alignment claims rely on circular reasoning (comparing against MT-Bench which uses LLM judges) and a marginal Spearman correlation difference (0.9955 vs 0.9699). No direct comparison against held-out human preference judgments

Model specification not validated: The multiplicative form σ(γ_k(s_i − s_j)) assumes uniform scaling of judge reliability across all score differences. No analysis of failure modes, when this assumption breaks, or robustness to systematic judge biases

Practical edge cases: Numerical instability for judges with γ ≈ 0 (one judge excluded in-house study). No principled approach to detecting or handling unreliable judges. Tie-as-0.5 encoding is ad-hoc with no sensitivity analysis

Modest practical improvements: Confidence interval width reductions are 13.5% (in-house) and 5.4% (Chatbot Arena). Efficiency gains in Figure 4 plateau at moderate sample sizes, limiting practical impact when abundant comparisons are available

Incomplete theoretical presentation: Explicit asymptotic covariance formula deferred to appendices. Finite-sample behavior under non-uniform comparison designs not explored. Some regularity conditions for Theorem 3.4 not fully stated
Limited parameter interpretation: Estimated γ values presented but not thoroughly investigated. No analysis of whether low γ values correlate with known problematic judges or systematic biases
Task-dependent judge reliability unaddressed: Judges may have different reliability across different tasks (acknowledged as future work but represents important practical limitation)
Reproducibility concerns: No code or data release mentioned. Algorithm A.1 not shown. Adam optimizer hyperparameters not specified. Limited details on newly collected dataset

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Judge reliability heterogeneity in LLM-as-a-judge is a genuine and under-addressed practical issue with clear motivation via the 'more data, more confidently wrong' phenomenon

Rigorous asymptotic theory: Establishes identifiability up to natural normalizations, proves consistency and asymptotic normality of MLE with explicit covariance, enabling valid confidence intervals—a genuine theoretical contribution

Simulation validation is compelling: Demonstrates critical advantage where weighted model maintains ~95% coverage while unweighted shows systematic under-coverage that worsens with sample size, validating O(1/√T) convergence rates

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple public benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback) plus newly collected in-house dataset; diverse judge panels; strong correlation with human preferences
Clear modeling framework: The judge-aware BTL extension is intuitive and mathematically well-presented; identifiability results are properly characterized
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Judge-specific discrimination parameters in ranking models are not new (Otani et al. 2016, IRT literature, Crowd-BT). The application to LLM evaluation is somewhat novel but feels incremental for a top-tier venue

Critical gap between theory and practice: Theory assumes i.i.d. uniform random design (Section 3.1), but experiments use sparse, non-uniform comparison graphs with dataset-specific structures and tie outcomes (Section 5.1). No analysis of whether asymptotic guarantees hold under realistic designs, undermining theoretical-practical connection

Modest empirical improvements in realistic settings: Table 1 shows both methods preserve identical MT-Bench ranking; Table 2 shows marginal Spearman improvement (0.9955 vs 0.9699); Figure 4 reveals methods nearly identical at realistic sample sizes; confidence interval reduction only 5.4-13.5%. Main gains confined to low-data regimes where practical utility is limited

Insufficient comparison with alternatives: REM, GTR/FTR, Crowd-BT, and Product-of-Experts mentioned but not empirically compared. Only baseline is unweighted BTL; missing opportunity to demonstrate advantage over other weighting schemes

Practical robustness concerns: One judge excluded due to numerical instability (Appendix F.3), raising questions about failure rates; tie encoding as y=0.5 lacks justification and sensitivity analysis; model only captures random noise, not systematic judge bias; boundary behavior (γk→0) unexplored

Limited scope of practical impact: The method's primary advantage appears in data-scarce regimes (Figure 4) where improvements are least needed. Organizations deploying LLM evaluation typically have sufficient budget for many comparisons, where both methods converge. High-impact applications likely outside method's sweet spot

Missing critical experimental analysis: Different judge panel sizes across datasets without systematic study; simulations assume true model is judge-aware BTL without robustness to other misspecifications; in-house dataset only 45 models; no exploration of when judge-aware modeling is necessary versus overhead

Theoretical-practical gaps in model specification: Logistic form with linear score difference relationship not justified; homogeneous discrimination structure within judges not discussed; no exploration of link function alternatives or misspecification robustness

Optimization and implementation clarity: Algorithm A.1 in appendix without convergence guarantees; Adam with projection constraints—are convergence guarantees preserved?; sensitivity to initialization unexplored; γ̂k estimate stability not thoroughly examined

Interpretability and diagnostics: Limited discussion of what γk heterogeneity means in real data; what causes variation in discrimination parameters?; how interpretable are estimated reliabilities; no guidance on when estimates are reliable versus unstable

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing heterogeneous judge reliability in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, with compelling motivation that ignoring heterogeneity leads to biased rankings and invalid uncertainty quantification
Solid theoretical contributions including identifiability (Theorem 3.2), consistency and asymptotic normality (Theorem 3.4) that enable principled confidence intervals for rankings
Rigorous empirical validation: simulation studies convincingly demonstrate O(1/√T) convergence rates, correct ~95% coverage for proposed method vs. systematic under-coverage for unweighted BTL

Comprehensive real-world evaluation on multiple benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, in-house dataset) showing consistent improvements in data efficiency (13.5% reduction in CI width) and recovery of known model rankings
Clear model formulation extending BTL with intuitive interpretation of judge discrimination parameters; clean mathematical presentation
Demonstrates practical impact: correctly recovers GPT-4 > Claude > GPT-3.5 ordering in Chatbot Arena where unweighted method fails; efficiency gains most pronounced in low-data regimes
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: modeling annotator/judge reliability is well-established (Crowd-BT, IRT models); main contributions are applying discrimination parameters to LLM setting and providing asymptotic theory, which is somewhat incremental

Model assumptions may be restrictive: uniform random design assumption not validated; constant judge discrimination across all model pairs ignores task/model-specific reliability; no allowance for judge-model interactions or serial dependencies

Numerical stability issues not adequately addressed: one judge with γ̂ ≈ 0 excluded due to instability; no systematic analysis of optimizer behavior at boundaries or frequency of instability in practice
Limited baseline comparisons: only compares against unweighted BTL; does not experimentally evaluate against REM, GTR, FTR, or other judge-weighting methods mentioned in related work

Ground truth validation limitations: MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena comparisons use published rankings not human preferences; UltraFeedback correlations are correlational; in-house study limited (45 models, 18 judges)

Incomplete practical guidance: no model selection advice for when to use judge-aware vs. unweighted BTL; minimum sample size requirements not discussed; handling of disconnected comparison graphs not addressed

Limited interpretation of learned judge reliabilities: γ̂k learned but not analyzed for what drives reliability; no investigation of correlation with judge properties; missing guidance for practitioners on improving judge quality

Identifiability and normalization concerns: normalization constraints affect score interpretation; sensitivity to normalization choice not discussed; why log-normalization for γ vs. alternatives not justified

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with complete asymptotic analysis (consistency, normality, identifiability, Fisher information invertibility) enabling principled uncertainty quantification for LLM rankings

Timely and important problem: judge heterogeneity in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is well-motivated and practically significant; the observation that 'more data makes evaluation more confidently wrong' under misspecification is insightful

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple datasets (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, in-house) with diverse judge pools; simulation study confirms theoretical predictions (O(1/T) rate, correct coverage)
Sound technical design: multiplicative discrimination parameterization γₖ is well-justified for LLM judges; clean identifiability characterization with natural normalizations
Strong practical results in data-limited regimes (Figure 4); consistent CI width reduction (5-13%); demonstrated stability of judge discrimination across datasets
Excellent reproducibility: complete algorithm, detailed simulations, multiple public datasets, code promised; thoughtful treatment of edge cases (ties, numerical stability, sparse designs)
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: extension of BTL with multiplicative parameters is relatively straightforward; proof techniques follow standard M-estimator theory; relationship to Crowd-BT and Otani et al. (2016) regarding novel contributions could be clearer

Model assumptions not thoroughly validated: conditional independence of judge errors is assumed but correlated errors among similar architectures not explored; scalar γₖ leaves task-specific variation unmodeled; Appendix F.6 extension shows negligible effects (ρ=0.9996)

Scope limitations: empirical evaluation entirely on LLM ranking despite general applicability claims; no human evaluation to validate that fitted scores align with human preferences; cannot address fundamental judge biases, only rescale them

Modest empirical improvements relative to unweighted baseline: CI width reductions of 5-13% are useful but not transformative; critically, no empirical comparison with cited related methods (REM, FTR) despite discussing them

Practical robustness concerns: numerical instability when γ̂ ≈ 0 (one judge excluded); performance degrades substantially under sparse designs (Pearson r=0.613 at spanning-tree level); API dependency on together.ai models; limited guidance on hyperparameter selection

Incomplete experimental analysis: missing ablations (judge prompt sensitivity, adversarial judge sets, skewed quality distributions); rank inference less developed than score inference; diagnostic procedures for detecting model misspecification not provided

strengths: Well-motivated problem: judge heterogeneity in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is important and under-studied
Rigorous theoretical foundation: identifiability theorem and asymptotic normality enable principled confidence intervals
Comprehensive empirical validation: simulation studies demonstrate the core issue (Fig. 2 under-coverage) and real-world experiments across 4+ datasets
Practical awareness: handles ties, sparse graphs, provides implementation details and reproducibility guidance
Clear problem formulation: the observation that more data can make evaluations 'more confidently wrong' under misspecification is compelling
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical novelty: discrimination-weighted BTL extends standard models with techniques from IRT literature; asymptotic theory applies standard M-estimator results without novel methodology
Modest empirical improvements: 5.4-13.5% CI width reduction is meaningful but not transformative; improvements concentrate in low-budget regimes untypical of real deployments

Restrictive assumptions often violated: (1) full-support design assumption fails with unbalanced sampling; (2) conditional independence of judge errors is violated by correlated biases and systematic preferences; (3) task-dependent variation (F.6 shows length extension yields 0.9996 correlation with base model)

Incomplete practical solutions: no guidance on choosing judge panel size K; judge selection procedure not systematized; cannot distinguish noisy from systematically biased judges; doesn't address correlated judge errors or temporal drift

Missing comparisons: no empirical comparison with weighted averaging, heuristic adaptive weighting, or Product-of-Experts aggregation; related Bayesian work (Fathullah & Gales 2025) mentioned but not compared

Limited impact on real decisions: paper demonstrates improved uncertainty quantification but not cases where judge-aware weighting produces materially different rankings affecting deployment decisions
Presentation issues: key results (Table 2, Figure 3 on judge heterogeneity) in appendices; in-house dataset description buried in appendix D.2 despite use in main efficiency results

Unresolved technical concerns: Fisher information invertibility assumes connected item graphs; convergence guarantees for non-convex Algorithm A.1 not provided; sensitivity to γ_k misspecification not tested

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in LLM evaluation: judge heterogeneity, with clear motivation that naive aggregation can lead to confidently wrong rankings

Rigorous theoretical contributions: establishes identifiability (Theorem 3.2), proves consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE (Theorem 3.4) enabling valid confidence intervals for LLM rankings

Comprehensive experimental validation: simulation studies validate O(1/T) convergence and confidence interval calibration; multiple real-world benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, in-house) show consistent improvements
Natural model extension with clear interpretation: the judge-aware BTL model γk(si - sj) elegantly captures judge discrimination differences without requiring ground truth

Practical improvements demonstrated: weighted aggregation achieves 5-13% CI width reduction, better alignment with human preferences (Chatbot Arena ρ=0.9955 vs 0.9699), and higher data efficiency in small-budget regimes
Well-written and well-structured paper with honest limitations discussion; strong emphasis on reproducibility with code to be released
Broader applicability beyond LLM evaluation to any pairwise comparison setting with multiple judges (crowdsourcing, expert panels, peer review)
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: adding discrimination parameter γk to BTL is a natural extension; related ideas appear in prior crowdsourcing (Crowd-BT) and IRT-based work, though authors do advance beyond prior work theoretically and in application domain

Modest empirical improvements concentrated in small-data regimes: while consistent, advantages narrow substantially as T increases (Figure 4); CI reduction of 5.4% on Chatbot Arena; most rank changes negligible in Table A.7; improvements may be most relevant for low-budget scenarios that practitioners may not face

Important model limitations acknowledged but not addressed: scalar judge discrimination γk constant across all pairs/tasks; no modeling of task-specific reliability, correlated judge errors, or systematic biases (Section 6 lists as future work but these are fundamental)

Restrictive modeling assumptions with practical implications: full-support random design assumption difficult to guarantee; connected comparison graph requirement; sparse designs show degradation (spanning-tree designs: ρ=0.044 yields Spearman 0.613 vs 0.927 for denser graphs)
Numerical stability issues: one judge (GLM-4.5-Air-FP8) had γ̂≈0 and required exclusion; no principled approach for handling extreme reliability estimates or adversarially poor judges

Limited baseline comparisons: primary comparison against unweighted BTL; incomplete empirical comparison with related methods (FTR, Product-of-Experts mentioned but not thoroughly compared); some circularity in using human evaluation as ground truth

Incomplete analysis of method behavior: limited failure case analysis; no discussion of when judge downweighting hurts; when does the method struggle with specific heterogeneity patterns; no statistical significance testing of empirical improvements
